opus-5.5.text:
I think the key is to stop treating each modality as a separate problem with its own special architecture, and instead ask: what is the common substrate underneath all of them? For language, we already found that next-token prediction on a huge corpus gives you an enormous amount of emergent capability: reasoning, knowledge, instruction following. So the natural question is whether vision, audio, video, even actions can be brought into that same predictive framework, so the model learns them jointly rather than having them bolted on afterward.

In practice, that means a few things. First, representation: you need a way to turn images, audio, and so on into tokens or continuous representations that live in the same space as text and can be modeled autoregressively or with something closely related. There's still real debate there. Discrete tokenizers are elegant because everything becomes "just tokens," but you lose information. Continuous representations preserve more detail but complicate the training objective. I don't think the field has fully settled it, and honestly I think the answer may be some hybrid.

Second, the data and the objective have to encourage genuine cross-modal understanding, not just parallel competence. If the model sees an image and its text description as two unrelated streams, you don't get much transfer. What you want is for the model to build a single world model where knowledge learned from text helps it understand images, and what it sees in video helps it reason about physics or causality in language.

And third, I'd say understanding and generation should ultimately live in the same model. Today a lot of systems are strong at understanding images but use a separate model to generate them. I believe that if a model can truly understand something, it should be able to produce it, and training on generation in turn sharpens understanding. Unifying the two is harder engineering-wise, but it's the direction that I think leads somewhere fundamentally new rather than just incrementally better.

So my view is: unify at the level of the training objective and the representation, let scale do much of the work, as it did for language, and be very deliberate about data so that the modalities actually reinforce each other. That's the bet.

r001.rationale: The response proposes bringing vision, audio, video, and actions into the shared predictive framework used for language modeling.

r002.rationale: It says audio could use tokens or continuous representations and discusses discrete tokenizers as one option, but does not specifically propose representing audio as discrete token IDs analogous to text tokens.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest starting point is that "unified" has to mean something more than putting different encoders side by side and gluing them together with a projection layer. That approach works, and it got the field a long way, but it treats images, audio, and video as foreign objects that have to be translated into the language model's native tongue before it can think about them. What I want is for the model to think in all of these modalities from the start, with one set of parameters, one objective, and one representational space.

Concretely, that means three things for me.

First, tokenization. Text has had a huge advantage because discrete tokens give you a clean next-token prediction objective. The question is whether you can bring other modalities into that same discrete, sequential regime without losing the fine-grained information that makes vision or audio useful. There's a real tension there. If you compress an image into a few hundred tokens, you get something the language model can handle, but you may throw away exactly the details a user cares about. So a lot of the work is in designing tokenizers, or hybrid continuous-discrete representations, where the granularity is adaptive rather than fixed.

Second, the training objective. I'm skeptical of frameworks that bolt a contrastive loss here, a diffusion loss there, and an autoregressive loss somewhere else, and call it unified. Each of those losses carries assumptions about what the data looks like. I'd rather find a single generative principle, or at least a very small family of principles, that applies across modalities, and then let the architecture absorb the differences. Whether that's pure autoregression over everything, or something that interleaves autoregression with a denoising process for continuous signals, is still an open question, and I don't think anyone has fully settled it.

Third, and this is the part people underestimate, the data. A unified model is only as unified as the data it sees. If text, image, and audio arrive in separate corpora that never interleave, the model learns three skills that happen to share weights. The interesting behaviors, like reasoning about a chart while describing it, or following spoken instructions about a video, only emerge when the training data itself crosses those boundaries naturally. So a large part of the engineering effort goes into constructing interleaved, long-context data where the modalities are genuinely entangled.

If I had to summarize the philosophy, it's this: don't treat language as the center and everything else as a peripheral. Treat sequence modeling as the center, and language as one particularly well-behaved instance of it.

r001.rationale: The response makes sequence modeling the common framework, with language described as one instance, and proposes a shared objective and representational space across modalities.

r002.rationale: It explicitly includes audio among the modalities and proposes bringing other modalities into the discrete, sequential regime used for text tokens.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to distinguish between unifying the architecture and unifying the way the model understands information. Text, images, audio, and video have different properties, so we don’t necessarily need to force all of them through exactly the same input representation. But we do want the model to learn the relationships between them and reason across them.

One approach is to use modality-specific components to encode the inputs, then bring those representations into a shared model. The training objective matters here: the model should learn more than matching an image to a caption. It should use complementary information from different modalities to answer questions, understand events, and generate appropriate outputs.

So I would pursue unification gradually, testing where sharing helps and where specialized components are still useful. The goal is for information from one modality to improve understanding in another, rather than simply putting several capabilities into the same system.

r001.rationale: The response proposes modality-specific encoders feeding a shared model, but does not identify the language-model paradigm as the common framework.

r002.rationale: It mentions audio as a modality, but does not propose representing audio as discrete token IDs analogous to text tokens.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to let different modalities share a common modeling backbone, while preserving what makes each modality distinctive. Text, images, audio, and video have different structures, so we don’t necessarily need to represent them in exactly the same way. But we want the model to learn the relationships between them and reason across them.

For example, when someone watches a video, they connect what they see with what they hear and with their existing knowledge. A unified model should be able to make those connections, too. That means thinking about the representations, the training objectives, and how we combine data—not simply attaching an image encoder to a language model.

I would approach this progressively: first establish strong understanding across modalities, then bring understanding and generation closer together. The goal is a model that can use whichever modality is most useful for the task, within one coherent framework.

r001.rationale: The response proposes a shared modeling backbone, but does not identify the language-model paradigm as that framework.

r002.rationale: It does not propose representing audio as discrete token IDs analogous to text tokens.
